title: Quebe v. United States
articleTitle: Exhaustive Report on United States v. Quebe: Implications for the R&D Tax Credit and Section 179D Deductions
court: United States District Court, Southern District of Ohio
subject: Substantiation of Qualified Research Expenses Under Section 41
summary: Quebe v. United States, litigated as United States v. Quebe in the Southern District of Ohio, disallowed an S corporation owner's Section 41 R&D tax credits and Section 179D deductions. The key takeaway for taxpayers who acquire legacy businesses: using the start-up base period requires admissible evidence that acquired predecessors lacked disqualifying 1984–1988 research history.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Overview of the Litigation and Procedural Posture

The federal district court litigation in United States v. Quebe, Case No. 3:15-cv-294 (S.D. Ohio), stands as a watershed judicial precedent in United States federal tax law governing the substantiation of the Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 and the Energy Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction under IRC Section 179D. Adjudicated across three pivotal rulings by the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio, Western Division at Dayton—specifically Magistrate Judge Sharon L. Ovington’s discovery sanctions order on May 16, 2017 (321 F.R.D. 303), which followed her January 23, 2017 order partially granting the Government’s motion to compel, District Judge Thomas M. Rose’s summary judgment order disallowing the Section 41 R&D tax credits on January 17, 2019 (2019 WL 250602, 123 AFTR 2d ¶2019-352), and Judge Rose’s companion summary judgment order disallowing the Section 179D deductions on January 25, 2019 (2019 WL 330852, 123 AFTR 2d 2019-543)—the case systematically dismantles aggressive, consultant-driven retroactive tax credit studies in the specialty construction and engineering contracting sectors.

Unusually for federal tax controversies, which typically arise as deficiency proceedings in the United States Tax Court or as taxpayer-initiated refund suits under 26 U.S.C. § 7422(a), Quebe was prosecuted by the United States Department of Justice as a civil action to recover erroneous refunds pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 7405(b). The defendants, Dennis F. Quebe and Linda G. Quebe, were a married couple filing joint federal individual income tax returns. At all relevant times, Dennis Quebe was the sole shareholder of Quebe Holdings, Inc. (QHI), an S corporation founded in 2002. Upon its formation in 2002, QHI acquired two established electrical contracting companies—Chapel Electric (Chapel) and Romanoff Electric (Romanoff)—through which, the Government argued, QHI had gross receipts and qualified research expenses both before 1984 and during the 1984–1988 statutory base period. In 2003, Dennis Quebe founded a third subsidiary, CRT Technologies (CRT). Because QHI elected passthrough S corporation status, all items of income, deduction, and tax credit generated by QHI and its operating subsidiaries flowed through to Dennis Quebe and were reported on the joint individual Forms 1040 filed with Linda Quebe.
Summary of the Taxpayers' Claims and the IRS Challenge

In September 2012, QHI engaged a tax services provider, Alliantgroup, LP (Alliant), to conduct a retroactive "Research and Development Tax Credit Study" for tax years 2008 to 2011, which concluded, in part, that QHI was entitled to claim Section 41 research credits and Section 179D energy-efficiency deductions for the 2009 and 2010 taxable years. Alliant agreed to be compensated to the extent that it determined QHI was eligible for the research credit, in an amount no greater than 25 percent of the tax credit ultimately identified. In their interrogatory responses in the subsequent litigation, the Quebes contended that QHI’s qualified research consisted of commercial electrical contracting activities, including developing new means and methods, issuing requests for information (RFIs), implementing change orders, conducting value engineering, determining pathways for conduit and wiring, coordinating among construction trades, and performing estimation; they separately asserted that QHI had a prefabrication unit in 2009–2010 and that its subsidiaries designed the prefabrication and modularization units integrated into the detailed electrical designs of several projects.

To compute the Section 41 Regular Research Credit on its amended 2009 and 2010 Form 1120S returns, QHI utilized the alternative "start-up company" base period computation under IRC § 41(c)(3)(B), which permitted QHI to apply a favorable fixed-base percentage of 3 percent rather than calculating a historical fixed-base percentage from 1984–1988 data. Simultaneously, QHI claimed deductions under IRC § 179D for the 2009 and 2010 tax years for installing energy-efficient lighting systems in nine commercial and public buildings, consisting of five buildings located on Wright-Patterson Air Force Base (WPAFB) and four newly constructed public school buildings.

Flowing from QHI’s amended S corporation returns, Dennis and Linda Quebe filed Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Returns (Forms 1040X) for tax years 2008, 2009, and 2010. The 2008 Form 1040X claimed a reduction in individual income tax liability of $87,054.00 resulting from the carryback from 2009 of a portion of the claimed Section 41 R&D tax credit. On August 26, 2013, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disbursed a refund of $119,954.65 to the Quebes, representing the refund claimed on their 2009 Form 1040X (which reflected a $107,292.00 reduction in tax liability) plus statutory overpayment interest, and on April 7, 2014, the IRS disbursed a refund of $129,482.90, representing the full refund claimed on their 2010 Form 1040X (which reflected a $118,048.00 reduction in tax liability) plus statutory overpayment interest. On August 25, 2015, the United States initiated suit under IRC § 7405(b) to recover the allegedly erroneous refunds.

The Government challenged the taxpayers' claims on two primary statutory fronts. With respect to the Section 41 R&D tax credit, the Government contended that because QHI, Chapel, Romanoff, and CRT constituted a single taxpayer under the controlled group and predecessor aggregation rules of IRC § 41(f), Chapel’s and Romanoff’s operational histories in the 1980s were legally imputed to QHI. Citing the very activities the Quebes claimed as "qualified research" in 2009 and 2010, the Government showed through deposition testimony that Chapel engaged in the same kinds of activities during the 1980s, and argued that QHI therefore had gross receipts and qualified research expenses both before 1984 and during the 1984–1988 period, barring it from the § 41(c)(3)(B) start-up company method, and that the Quebes failed to substantiate their claim for the credit. With respect to the Section 179D deduction, the Government asserted that none of the lighting fixtures in the five WPAFB buildings were actually "placed in service" during 2009, and that QHI was merely an electrical installer—not the "person primarily responsible for designing the property"—with respect to the four public school buildings.
Governing Statutory Framework and Final Judicial Holdings
The District Court evaluated the controversy under the interlocking provisions of the Internal Revenue Code, Treasury Regulations, and Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and Evidence.

Disposition in United States v. Quebe

cells: IRC § 41(a)(1) & § 41(c)(1)
Establishes a 20% credit for current-year QREs exceeding a historical "base amount" derived from the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage and prior four-year average annual gross receipts.
Disallowed in full; QHI failed to substantiate a valid base amount computation.
IRC § 41(c)(3)(A) vs. § 41(c)(3)(B)

Prescribes the standard 1984–1988 base period for established taxpayers (§ 41(c)(3)(A)) versus the alternative "start-up" method (§ 41(c)(3)(B)), available only if the first taxable year in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and QREs began after 1983, or if there were fewer than three years between 1984 and 1988 in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and QREs.
Court held QHI failed to prove eligibility for the § 41(c)(3)(B) start-up base period given acquired subsidiaries' 1980s operations.
IRC § 41(f)(1) & § 41(f)(3)

Mandates that all members of a controlled group of corporations or trades/businesses under common control be treated as a single taxpayer, and attributes the historical gross receipts and QREs of acquired predecessors to the acquiring taxpayer.
Applied strictly; Chapel, Romanoff, CRT, and QHI were aggregated as a single taxpayer, imputing 1980s contracting history to QHI.
Defines "qualified research" via the Four-Part Test at the business component level and excludes research to the extent "funded" by any grant, contract, or another person.
Taxpayers' attempt to reclassify 1980s predecessor work as excluded "funded research" (Time & Materials) failed for lack of admissible evidence.
IRC § 6001 & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)
Obligates taxpayers to keep permanent books and records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate entitlement to any claimed tax credit.
Enforced to defeat the claim; the taxpayers offered no admissible evidence regarding their predecessors' 1980s operations to substantiate start-up base period eligibility.
IRC § 7405(b)
Authorizes the United States to bring a civil action in federal district court to recover any portion of a tax refund erroneously made.
Government satisfied its ultimate burden under § 7405(b) by proving the taxpayers lacked admissible evidence to substantiate their credit.
IRC § 179D & IRS Notice 2008-40

Allows a deduction for energy-efficient commercial building property in the year "placed in service," allocable by government owners to the person "primarily responsible" for designing the property (Notice 2008-40 permits the owner, at its discretion, to allocate among several designers, but excludes a person who merely installs the property).
Disallowed in full; WPAFB fixtures were not placed in service in 2009, and QHI was an installer rather than the primary designer on school projects.

body.text: Ultimately, the District Court granted summary judgment to the United States on all counts. By holding that the deposition testimony of Alliant’s corporate representative was inadmissible hearsay and that the taxpayer retains the underlying burden of substantiating base period eligibility even in a Government-initiated erroneous refund suit, Judge Rose invalidated the entirety of QHI’s Section 41 R&D tax credits for 2009 and 2010, while the Section 179D deductions were disallowed in a separate order on placed-in-service and designer grounds.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
Controlled Group Aggregation and Predecessor M&A Taint in Base Period Computations

The foundational legal failure in Quebe stemmed from a disregard of how corporate acquisitions interact with the incremental mechanics of the Regular Research Credit under IRC § 41(a)(1) and § 41(f). Because Congress designed the Section 41 credit (originally enacted in 1981 and made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015) to incentivize incremental increases in research spending over time rather than to subsidize static baseline operations, a taxpayer claiming the Regular Research Credit must establish its historical "base amount". Under IRC § 41(c)(1), the base amount is calculated by multiplying the taxpayer’s "fixed-base percentage" by the average annual gross receipts of the taxpayer for the four taxable years preceding the credit year, subject to a statutory floor where the base amount cannot be less than 50 percent of current-year QREs.

Under the default rule of IRC § 41(c)(3)(A), an established taxpayer’s fixed-base percentage is the ratio of its aggregate QREs for the taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989 (the 1984–1988 base period) to its aggregate gross receipts for those same years. Recognizing that newly formed enterprises or companies that did not conduct R&D alongside revenue generation in the 1980s could not compute a 1984–1988 ratio, Congress enacted the alternative "start-up company" rules in IRC § 41(c)(3)(B). Under § 41(c)(3)(B)(i), a taxpayer qualifies to use the start-up company method only if the first taxable year in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and QREs began after December 31, 1983, or if there were fewer than three taxable years during the 1984–1988 period in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and QREs. For its first five qualified years beginning after 1993, a qualifying start-up company is assigned a fixed-base percentage of just 3 percent under IRC § 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(I).

When preparing QHI’s retroactive 2009 and 2010 R&D credit claims, Alliant treated QHI as a start-up company under § 41(c)(3)(B), assigning QHI the 3 percent fixed-base percentage. This computational shortcut ignored the combined operation of IRC § 41(f)(1) (aggregation of controlled groups and businesses under common control) and IRC § 41(f)(3) (consistency and predecessor rules for acquisitions and dispositions). Under § 41(f)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6, QHI (founded in 2002), Chapel (acquired in 2002), Romanoff (acquired in 2002), and CRT (founded in 2003) were treated as a single, unified taxpayer in computing the research credit. Furthermore, under the acquisition rules of § 41(f)(3)(A), when a taxpayer acquires the major portion of a trade or business of another person, the QREs and gross receipts of the acquiring taxpayer for periods before the acquisition must be increased by the QREs and gross receipts of the predecessor attributable to the acquired business.

Because the Government showed that Chapel was performing electrical contracting work in the 1980s and argued that QHI, through Chapel and Romanoff, had gross receipts and QREs both before 1984 and during the 1984–1988 base period, QHI stepped directly into their 1980s tax history. Consequently, QHI could only utilize the 3 percent start-up fixed-base percentage if it could prove with admissible evidence that neither Chapel nor Romanoff incurred QREs while generating gross receipts prior to 1984 or in three or more years between 1984 and 1988. By failing to account for the M&A tax history of Chapel and Romanoff—or alternatively by failing to elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(4), which calculates a 14 percent credit above 50 percent of the rolling three-year prior QRE average and completely bypasses the 1984–1988 base period—QHI walked into an insurmountable historical substantiation trap.
The Symmetry Trap in Defining Qualified Research Under the Four-Part Test

A critical second-order implication of Quebe is how an overly expansive definition of "qualified research" in the claim years creates a fatal "symmetry trap" under the consistency mandate of the Internal Revenue Code. Under IRC § 41(d)(1), activities constitute "qualified research" only if they satisfy a stringent Four-Part Test applied separately to each "business component" (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)): the expenditures must be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 (requiring the elimination of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component); the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature (relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science); the application of that information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component (focused on function, performance, reliability, or quality); and substantially all (at least 80 percent) of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation. Crucially, the base period consistency rule requires that QREs taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage for the 1984–1988 base period be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year.

In their interrogatory responses defending the 2009 and 2010 credit claims, the Quebes asserted that a broad spectrum of commercial electrical contracting operations constituted qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(1). Specifically, the Quebes contended that QHI’s 2009 and 2010 qualified research encompassed developing new means and methods, issuing RFIs, implementing change orders, performing value engineering, determining pathways for conduit and wiring, coordinating among trades, and performing estimation, and they separately pointed to QHI’s prefabrication and modularization work. During discovery, the Government elicited deposition testimony from Dennis Quebe, as QHI’s corporate representative, that Chapel resolved uncertainties related to developing means and methods during the 1980s, determined the routing for conduit and wiring in the 1980s, and engaged in trade coordination in the 1980s, and that he himself worked as an estimator in the early 1980s; Mr. Quebe further testified that he did not know whether Chapel performed value engineering in the 1980s but had reason to believe it did.

This placed the taxpayers in an inescapable logical dilemma. If routine electrical contracting activities such as value engineering, conduit routing, trade coordination, RFI issuance, and developing means and methods genuinely satisfied the Four-Part Test of IRC § 41(d) in 2009 and 2010, then under the consistency rule, those identical activities constituted qualified research when performed by Chapel during 1984–1988. That meant QHI had both gross receipts and QREs throughout 1984–1988, disqualifying it from the § 41(c)(3)(B) start-up method and requiring QHI to prove its exact 1984–1988 QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio under § 41(c)(3)(A)—which it did not do, because it offered no admissible evidence of how much its predecessors spent on research in the base period relative to their gross receipts. Conversely, if Chapel’s 1984–1988 electrical contracting activities did not constitute qualified research because they were routine commercial adaptation (excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B)), duplication (excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C)), or standard trade work lacking a structured process of experimentation, then QHI’s identical 2009 and 2010 activities failed the Four-Part Test under IRC § 41(d) as well. Although the Quebes asserted that Chapel did not have a prefabrication division during 1984–1988 (a prefabrication division providing an offsite space for electrical engineers to test different wiring solutions), this assertion could not rescue their start-up status; the court found that, apart from the inadmissible testimony of Alliant’s corporate representative, the evidence cited by the Quebes went only to whether QHI conducted qualifying research in 2009 and 2010, leaving nothing to rebut the Government’s showing that QHI, through Chapel, engaged in the same kinds of activities in the 1980s.
Contractual Risk Allocation and the Unsubstantiated Funded Research Exclusion Defense

Confronted with the reality that Chapel performed identical electrical contracting activities in the 1980s, the taxpayers attempted to rescue their start-up status by invoking the "funded research" exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) as an offensive weapon to erase their 1980s QREs. Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), qualified research does not include any research to the extent it is funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. Under the governing two-prong regulatory framework applied in federal case law—including Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), and subsequently Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024)—research performed for a customer under contract is excluded as "funded" unless the contractor both bears the financial risk of failure (meaning payment is contingent on the technical success of the research) and retains substantial rights in the research results.

Citing Geosyntec for the proposition that Time and Materials (T&M) based contracts are routinely found not to qualify for the Section 41 credit under the funding exclusion, the Quebes asserted that during the 1980s Chapel was engaged primarily in T&M contracts, wherein the customer paid for actual labor hours and materials expended regardless of technical outcome. Because T&M contracts generally place the financial risk of failure on the customer rather than the contractor, the Quebes disputed that Chapel and Romanoff had any QREs in the 1980s, effectively contending that Chapel’s 1980s activities were excluded as funded research under § 41(d)(4)(H). In contrast, the Quebes asserted that QHI’s 2009 and 2010 projects were performed predominantly under fixed-fee contracts, which purportedly placed financial risk on QHI and qualified as unfunded research.

This contractual defense collapsed because the Quebes supported it solely with inadmissible testimony rather than contemporaneous documentary evidence. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), determining whether research is funded requires an examination of the specific contractual terms governing payment risk, acceptance criteria, inspection, remedies for defective performance, and intellectual property rights entered into before the performance of the research. The Quebes’ T&M assertion rested solely on the deposition testimony of Alliant’s corporate representative; they offered no 1984–1988 contracts, billing ledgers, job cost reports, or corporate records from Chapel or Romanoff establishing that their 1980s work was performed under T&M contracts. Even if a single fixed-price contract involving qualified research had been executed by Chapel in each of three years between 1984 and 1988, QHI would have been disqualified from the start-up method. Without admissible evidence, the taxpayers’ assertion that Chapel’s historical operations were primarily T&M-based could not create a genuine issue of material fact.
Burden of Proof Architecture in Erroneous Refund Litigation and the 40-Year Recordkeeping Mandate

A central doctrinal holding of Quebe concerns the interplay between the Government’s burden of proof in an erroneous refund suit under IRC § 7405(b) and the taxpayer’s substantive recordkeeping and substantiation duties under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d). In opposing the Government’s motion for summary judgment, the Quebes argued—at least implicitly—that the United States bore the burden of proving that QHI (through Chapel and Romanoff) did engage in qualified research during 1984–1988 and therefore was not entitled to claim the credit.

Judge Rose squarely rejected this burden-shifting theory. The court acknowledged that in an action brought under IRC § 7405(b), the Government bears the ultimate burden of proving that a tax refund was erroneous and the extent of the erroneous refund. However, citing the United States Supreme Court’s holding in INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79, 84 (1992)—which describes deductions as a matter of legislative grace—Judge Rose emphasized that the taxpayer has the burden of showing its right to any claimed tax benefit. Under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(a) and (e), every taxpayer is required to keep permanent books of account or records sufficient to establish the amount of gross income, deductions, credits, or other matters required to be shown on any return. Specifically with respect to the research credit, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d) (and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d)) mandates that a taxpayer claiming the credit "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit".

Harmonizing § 7405(b) with § 6001 under the summary judgment standard of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56, the court held that the Government satisfies its affirmative burden in an erroneous refund suit by demonstrating that the taxpayer lacks admissible evidence to substantiate an essential statutory prerequisite of the claimed credit. Because demonstrating a valid base amount under IRC § 41(c) is an indispensable element of establishing entitlement to the Section 41 credit, the Quebes were legally obligated to come forward with affirmative, admissible evidence proving that QHI satisfied the statutory criteria for the § 41(c)(3)(B) start-up base period.

This ruling exposes two profound structural hazards for United States corporate taxpayers. First, it imposes a "double burden" of proving a historical negative: when an acquiring company claims the Regular Research Credit using the start-up method after acquiring legacy targets, the taxpayer must prove affirmatively that its current-year projects satisfy the Four-Part Test and QRE rules, and it must prove negatively—using admissible historical evidence—that its acquired predecessors did not incur QREs during the 1984–1988 base period. Second, it creates a "40-year shelf life" documentation problem: because QHI was formed in 2002 and acquired Chapel and Romanoff that same year, the relevant 1984–1988 base period records pre-dated QHI’s existence by nearly two decades. To defend a 2009–2010 credit claim litigated through 2019 (or a current credit claim in 2026), Chapel and Romanoff would have needed to preserve detailed contract and project records from 1984 through 2002, and QHI would have had to acquire and archive those records for another 17 to 24 years. Despite the practical difficulty of retaining 40-year-old subcontractor job files, the court held that the absence of admissible base period evidence operates against the taxpayer—a result consistent with principles established in prior substantiation cases such as Research, Inc. v. United States and Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, although the Quebe court did not itself cite those cases.
Evidentiary Inadmissibility of Contingent-Fee Consultant Testimony

The proximate cause of QHI’s defeat at summary judgment was its reliance on the deposition testimony of its third-party tax consultant rather than first-hand fact witnesses and contemporaneous business records. To establish that Chapel and Romanoff did not engage in qualified research in the 1980s and that Chapel was engaged primarily in T&M contracts during that period, the Quebes relied solely on the deposition testimony of Rizwan Husain Virani, the designated corporate representative of Alliant. The Quebes cited Mr. Virani’s deposition testimony for the assertion that QHI’s subsidiaries were not engaged in qualified research activities during the 1980s.

Judge Rose held that Mr. Virani’s testimony was inadmissible hearsay that could not be used to demonstrate the existence of a genuine issue of material fact under Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(2). Under Rule 56(c)(4) and Federal Rule of Evidence 602, testimony used to support or oppose a motion for summary judgment must be made on personal knowledge and set out facts that would be admissible in evidence. Mr. Virani did not have personal knowledge of QHI, much less of the business operations, engineering practices, or contract structures conducted by Chapel and Romanoff during the 1980s. Lacking such personal knowledge, his assertions regarding 1980s operations could only repeat information obtained from others. Offering a consultant’s secondhand account to prove the truth of what occurred in the 1980s constituted inadmissible hearsay (see Federal Rules of Evidence 801 and 802). Separately, in its recitation of the background facts, the court noted that Alliant had agreed to be compensated to the extent it determined QHI was eligible for the research credit, in an amount no greater than 25 percent of the credit ultimately identified, although the court did not rely on this fee arrangement in finding Mr. Virani’s testimony inadmissible. Once Mr. Virani’s testimony was excluded as inadmissible hearsay, the remaining evidence offered by the Quebes addressed only QHI’s contracting activities in 2009 and 2010, leaving no admissible evidence from which a factfinder could infer that QHI, through Chapel and Romanoff, did not engage in qualifying research in the 1980s.
Discovery Misconduct, Unverified Interrogatories, and Document Dump Sanctions

Long before Judge Rose entered summary judgment in January 2019, the taxpayers’ substantiation posture was severely compromised during discovery, culminating in Magistrate Judge Sharon L. Ovington’s published sanctions opinion in United States v. Quebe, 321 F.R.D. 303 (S.D. Ohio May 16, 2017), which enforced her earlier January 23, 2017 order compelling discovery. This ruling is cited directly by the IRS Office of Chief Counsel in Field Attorney Advice / Chief Counsel Advice Memorandum 20214101F as foundational authority governing the evidentiary specificity required for Section 41 research credit refund claims.

During discovery, the United States served written interrogatories and requests for production seeking the specific factual nexus required by IRC § 41(d): the identification of each business component claimed for 2009 and 2010, the specific research activities performed on each business component, the individuals who performed those activities, and the exact documents and QREs corresponding to each component. In response, the Quebes committed three severe procedural violations under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. First, violating Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(b)(4) and 34(b)(2)(B), the defendants prefaced their discovery responses with boilerplate "laundry list" objections asserting vagueness and undue burden without providing a detailed explanation of why the interrogatories were objectionable. Second, when ordered to identify the specific documents substantiating their qualified research activities and QREs, the defendants executed a "document dump," producing a massive volume of unorganized project records without specifying which records corresponded to which interrogatories or business components. Third, the defendants failed to have a party representative verify the accuracy of the interrogatory answers under oath as required by Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(b).

Magistrate Judge Ovington held that a taxpayer cannot use a high-volume document production to evade its obligation to link specific evidence to specific statutory claims. As the IRS subsequently emphasized in CCA 20214101F citing Quebe, "a mere volume of documents will not suffice to meet a taxpayer's obligation". Pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(b)(2)(C), the court sanctioned the defendants by ordering them to respond to Interrogatories 2 and 11 by May 31, 2017, and requiring them to pay the Government’s reasonable fees and expenses caused by their failure to comply with the January 23, 2017 order, while extending the discovery deadline to June 30, 2017 and the summary judgment motion deadline to July 31, 2017, rather than granting the default judgment or evidence-preclusion order the Government had requested. Discovery then closed on June 30, 2017, after the resolution of the interrogatory dispute, fixing the factual record on which the parties moved for summary judgment on July 31, 2017.
Complementary Technical Disqualification Under IRC Section 179D

In electrical and MEP contracting, consulting firms frequently bundle Section 41 R&D tax credit studies with Section 179D Energy Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction studies on the exact same construction projects. In United States v. Quebe, 2019 WL 330852 (S.D. Ohio Jan. 25, 2019), Judge Rose addressed QHI’s claimed 2009 and 2010 Section 179D deductions for installing energy-efficient lighting systems in five buildings at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base (WPAFB) and four public school buildings, exposing two additional legal and technical failures.

First, regarding the five WPAFB buildings, IRC § 179D(a) permits a taxpayer to deduct the cost of energy-efficient commercial building property only in the taxable year in which the property is "placed in service". QHI claimed a partial Section 179D deduction on its 2009 tax return based on an allocation letter—apparently prepared by a Chapel representative and signed in December 2012 by a Chapel representative and a WPAFB maintenance officer—stating an April 2009 in-service date, even though construction records established that none of the lighting fixtures were actually placed in service in 2009. Accepting the Government’s argument that it did not matter whether the military official was mistaken about the date, intended to allow the defendants to take the deduction in 2009, or simply failed to read the document carefully before signing it, Judge Rose stated that "U.S. military personnel cannot authorize taxpayers to claim tax deductions that they would not otherwise receive" because "[t]he United States is not bound by unauthorized acts of its agents". The court also refused to empanel a jury or issue an advisory opinion allowing QHI to claim the deductions in subsequent years, holding that the taxpayers’ sole remedy was to file a new administrative refund claim with the IRS for the years the fixtures were actually placed in service.

Second, regarding the four public school buildings, IRC § 179D(d)(4) and IRS Notice 2008-40 provide that for government-owned buildings, the deduction may be allocated, in lieu of the owner, to the "person primarily responsible for designing the property". On the school projects, third-party architects and engineers had created the technical design specifications, while QHI selected fixtures meeting those specifications and installed the lighting systems. Judge Rose rejected the Quebes’ argument that the "primarily responsible" rule was arbitrary or that Notice 2008-40 expanded the deduction beyond what Congress authorized, holding that the rule is based on the statutory language drafted by Congress as elucidated by the IRS and that a contractor who merely installs the property is not a designer eligible for the Section 179D deduction.

Start-Up Company Base Period Eligibility

Taxpayer must affirmatively prove with admissible evidence that the aggregated group (including predecessors) did not have both gross receipts and QREs prior to 1984 or in three or more years during 1984–1988.
Base Period Consistency & Four-Part Test Symmetry

Funded Research Exclusion (Historical vs. Current Contracts)
IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d); Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330.

Asserted that Chapel's 1980s work was excluded as "funded research" because Chapel was engaged primarily in Time & Materials (T&M) contracts while 2009–2010 work was predominantly fixed-fee, relying solely on the deposition testimony of Alliant's corporate representative and producing no 1980s contracts or ledgers.

Whether research is "funded" requires contract-specific proof of payment risk and IP rights; an assertion regarding 1980s T&M contract structures resting solely on inadmissible hearsay creates no genuine issue of material fact (the court did not rule on the merits of the funding exclusion).
Burden of Proof in Erroneous Refund Suits
IRC § 7405(b); IRC § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d); INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79.
Argued that the United States bore the burden under § 7405(b) to prove QHI did conduct qualified research in 1984–1988 to invalidate the start-up election.

While the Government bears the ultimate burden under § 7405(b) to show a refund was erroneous, the taxpayer always bears the underlying burden under § 6001 and INDOPCO to substantiate every element of a credit.
Admissibility of Summary Judgment Evidence
Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(2); see also Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(4); Fed. R. Evid. 602, 801, 802.

Relied solely on the deposition of Alliant's corporate representative (Rizwan Virani) to prove 1980s operations, despite Virani having no personal knowledge and Alliant holding a contingent financial interest.
Testimony from a third-party consultant hired decades later who lacks personal knowledge of QHI or its subsidiaries' historical operations is inadmissible hearsay and cannot defeat summary judgment.
Discovery Specificity & Business Component Nexus
Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(b)(4), 33(d), 34(b)(2)(B), 37(b); IRC § 41(d)(2); United States v. Quebe, 321 F.R.D. 303.
Served unverified responses with boilerplate objections and executed a massive "document dump" rather than mapping records and QREs to specific business components.

Volume of records does not equal substantiation; taxpayers must organize and index evidence linking specific individuals, uncertainties, and QREs to distinct business components or face Rule 37 sanctions.
Section 179D "Placed in Service" Timing & Sovereign Agency
IRC § 179D(a); federal agency authority doctrine.
Claimed 2009 partial deductions for five WPAFB buildings based on a military official's signed allocation letter despite fixtures not being placed in service until after 2009.

Deductions are strictly limited to the tax year property is actually placed in service; unauthorized or erroneous signatures by military/government personnel cannot bind the United States or waive tax law.
Section 179D "Primarily Responsible Designer" Test
IRC § 179D(d)(4); IRS Notice 2008-40.
Claimed § 179D deductions on four public schools where third-party architects/engineers created the specifications and QHI merely installed the lighting systems.

Government building allocations are restricted to designers who create the technical energy-efficient design specifications, with the deduction going to the person "primarily responsible" unless the owner allocates it among several designers; mere installers do not qualify.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of United States v. Quebe into actionable tax and engineering governance, the following two applied case studies examine realistic corporate taxpayers confronting the exact statutory, contractual, and evidentiary hazards that invalidated QHI’s tax benefits. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the court’s objections and satisfy IRC Sections 41 and 179D.
Case Study 1: Multi-Entity Electrical and MEP Design-Build Contractor Growing via Legacy Acquisitions
Fact Pattern and Exposure to Quebe Pitfalls

Apex Modular MEP Holdings, Inc. ("Apex Holdings") is an S corporation founded in 2018 that provides commercial electrical contracting, microgrid integration, and modular prefabrication services across the Midwest. In 2020, Apex Holdings acquired 100 percent of the stock of Tri-State Electrical Contractors, Inc. ("Tri-State"), a regional electrical subcontractor founded in 1978 that operated continuously throughout the 1984–1988 base period. In 2025, Apex Holdings engaged in two major capital projects. Under Project Alpha (Municipal University Hospital Microgrid & Modular MEP Corridor Racks), a $28 million construction contract, Apex Holdings engineered and fabricated custom, multi-trade modular headwall and overhead MEP corridor racks integrated with a hospital-wide islanding microgrid controller designed to achieve seamless sub-cycle transfer (<4 milliseconds) between utility power, photovoltaic arrays, and Tier 4 backup generators without disrupting sensitive MRI and surgical equipment. Under Project Beta (State University Science Complex LED & HVAC Controls), a $12 million subcontract with a general contractor, Apex Holdings installed high-efficiency LED lighting and building automation sensors across three state university buildings, seeking a $1.8 million Section 179D deduction alongside Section 41 R&D credits.

A contingent-fee tax credit consultant has proposed claiming $1.4 million in Section 41 Regular Research Credits for Apex Holdings on an amended return using the 3 percent "start-up company" fixed-base percentage under IRC § 41(c)(3)(B), capturing 100 percent of project managers’, estimators’, and field foremen’s wages spent on RFIs, change orders, Building Information Modeling (BIM) clash detection, trade coordination, and conduit routing. The consultant also prepared a Section 179D allocation letter signed by a university facilities manager listing a December 2025 placed-in-service date, even though final commissioning and occupancy occurred in February 2026. Left uncorrected, Apex Holdings faces total disallowance under every holding of United States v. Quebe.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Base Period Governance and Election of the Alternative Simplified Credit (IRC § 41(c)(4))

To neutralize the Quebe predecessor base-period trap under IRC § 41(f)(1) and § 41(f)(3)(A), Apex Holdings must immediately reject the consultant’s recommendation to claim the Regular Research Credit (RRC) "start-up company" method under IRC § 41(c)(3)(B). Because Tri-State operated between 1984 and 1988 and its historical operations are imputed to Apex Holdings under § 41(f), Apex Holdings would be forced to prove a historical negative—that Tri-State incurred zero QREs during 1984–1988—using 40-year-old contracts and accounting records that no longer exist. Instead, Apex Holdings must affirmatively elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(4) on Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) attached to its timely filed original return (or on an amended return pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(b)(2) provided an RRC was not previously claimed for that tax year). Under the ASC method, Apex Holdings calculates its credit as 14 percent of current-year QREs that exceed 50 percent of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years:

If the aggregated controlled group had zero QREs in any of the three preceding tax years, the statutory ASC rate is 6 percent of current-year QREs. By electing the ASC, Apex Holdings legally eliminates the 1984–1988 base period from the statutory calculation, restricting its historical substantiation obligation to the immediately preceding three tax years (2022–2024), for which complete digital accounting, payroll, and project records are readily available.
Step 2: Project Governance, Business Component Isolation, and Shrinking-Back Execution (IRC § 41(d)(2) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2))

To avoid the Quebe "symmetry trap" and satisfy the specificity standards of United States v. Quebe, 321 F.R.D. 303, and IRS CCA 20214101F, Apex Holdings must purge all routine electrical contracting activities from its R&D claim. Apex Holdings must institute a formal R&D Tax Governance Charter that explicitly excludes commercial estimation, standard RFI processing, administrative change orders, routine field conduit routing, and standard MEP trade coordination. Rather than claiming the entire $28 million Hospital construction contract as a single business component, Apex Holdings must apply the "shrinking-back" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to isolate the exact technical subsets where capability or design uncertainty existed at the outset of the project. Specifically, Apex Holdings will isolate two discrete business components: Business Component 1A (Sub-Cycle Microgrid Islanding Control Algorithm & Switchgear Logic), covering the hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation, relay logic programming, and harmonic distortion testing required to achieve <4ms seamless transfer without tripping hospital life-safety inverters; and Business Component 1B (Seismic-Rated High-Density Modular MEP Rack Pilot Model), covering the structural finite element analysis (FEA), thermal dissipation modeling, and physical destructive/load testing of the custom prefabricated multi-trade corridor rack prototype under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). All direct W-2 wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)) and prototype supply costs (IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)) must be tracked in separate sub-ledger job cost codes mapped exclusively to Business Components 1A and 1B, cleanly segregating experimental pre-production design and prototype testing from post-design commercial shop fabrication and field installation (which are excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A)).
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring to Defeat the Funded Research Exclusion (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d))

To ensure that its current-year engineering on Project Alpha is not disqualified as "funded research" under Fairchild, Geosyntec, and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Apex Holdings must restructure its commercial design-build contracts prior to executing project work. First, to satisfy the payment-risk prong of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), Apex Holdings must replace any Time & Materials (T&M) or cost-plus reimbursement provisions for the engineering and prototype phases with a Fixed-Price, Milestone-Contingent Design-Build Agreement containing an explicit performance guarantee. The contract must stipulate that payment for the microgrid controller and modular rack engineering is strictly contingent upon passing Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) and Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) demonstrating the <4ms transfer specification, with Apex Holdings bearing full financial responsibility to re-engineer, replace, or refund payments at its own expense if the technical parameters are not achieved. Second, to satisfy the substantial-rights prong, Apex Holdings must remove boilerplate "work-made-for-hire" clauses that vest exclusive intellectual property ownership in the hospital owner, substituting an explicit Intellectual Property Clause stating that Apex Holdings retains all right, title, and interest in its foreground engineering methodologies, modular rack structural designs, and control algorithms, while granting the hospital owner a non-exclusive, perpetual license to operate the installed systems at the project site.
Step 4: Section 179D Compliance and Statutory Timing Controls (Project Beta)

To prevent a repeat of the Quebe Section 179D summary judgment defeat (2019 WL 330852), Apex Holdings must overhaul its handling of Project Beta. Under IRC § 179D(d)(4) and IRS Notice 2008-40, because a third-party architectural and engineering firm authored the lighting and HVAC specifications on the State University buildings and Apex Holdings merely purchased and installed the specified fixtures, Apex Holdings is an installer rather than the "person primarily responsible for designing the property" and must decline to claim the § 179D deduction on those buildings. For future public building projects where Apex Holdings seeks a valid § 179D allocation, it must execute a Design-Build or Energy Performance Contract in which Apex Holdings’ in-house Professional Engineers (PEs) are contractually designated to create, stamp, and seal the technical energy-efficiency specifications and photometric/thermal models from inception. Furthermore, regarding the timing requirement of IRC § 179D(a), Apex Holdings must never rely on a government official’s accommodation signature listing an erroneous placed-in-service date. On any qualified design-build project where commissioning occurs in February 2026, Apex Holdings must require the government representative to execute an Allocation Letter reflecting the true February 2026 placed-in-service date (corroborated by the Certificate of Substantial Completion and occupancy permit) and claim the deduction strictly on its 2026 tax return.
Step 5: Contemporaneous Experimentation Tracking and Evidentiary Indexing

To eliminate the hearsay trap that invalidated Alliant’s testimony in Quebe and satisfy the Form 6765 / CCA 20214101F specificity standards, Apex Holdings must implement a bi-weekly project time-tracking system in which engineers and BIM modelers record hours directly against specific Business Component codes (BC-1A and BC-1B) alongside a mandatory text field capturing the technical uncertainty addressed, the hypothesis evaluated, and the simulation or test executed. Any R&D tax credit study or litigation declaration must be verified and signed under penalty of perjury by Apex Holdings’ Vice President of Engineering—a fact witness with direct personal knowledge under Fed. R. Evid. 602—rather than relying on a third-party consultant as the evidentiary declarant. Finally, Apex Holdings must maintain a digital, Bates-indexed audit binder linking every dollar of claimed W-2 wages and supplies to the exact employee, business component, engineering test log, FEA simulation file, and fixed-price contract, preventing any discovery sanctions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(b).
Case Study 2: Industrial Automation and Custom Control Systems Engineering Firm with Historical T&M Predecessors
Fact Pattern and Exposure to Quebe Pitfalls

Vanguard Automation Group, Inc. ("Vanguard") is a C corporation formed in 2015 that designs and manufactures custom robotic assembly cells and machine-vision inspection software for aerospace and medical device manufacturers. Between 2016 and 2019, Vanguard acquired three legacy industrial control-panel integration companies ("Legacy Subsidiaries") that had been in business since 1981. For the 2024 and 2025 tax years, Vanguard incurred approximately $18 million in annual QREs. Because Vanguard’s QREs surged dramatically in 2024 and 2025 compared to 2021–2023, Vanguard’s Tax Director calculated that the Regular Research Credit (20 percent rate under IRC § 41(a)(1)) would yield $950,000 more in federal tax credits per year than the Alternative Simplified Credit (14 percent rate under IRC § 41(c)(4))—provided Vanguard can substantiate that its Legacy Subsidiaries’ 1984–1988 activities were excluded as "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) because the Legacy Subsidiaries historically worked on Time & Materials (T&M) service contracts.

Simultaneously, in its current-year operations, Vanguard executes Master Services Agreements (MSAs) with aerospace clients that blend fixed-price prototype development with T&M field integration and software debugging, without clearly separating the billing or IP ownership terms. Furthermore, during a preliminary IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) Information Document Request (IDR), Vanguard’s external accountant responded by uploading 45,000 pages of raw ERP dumps, engineering drawings, and customer invoices into a shared folder without an index linking the documents to specific business components. Vanguard is positioned to suffer the exact dual catastrophe of United States v. Quebe: audit disallowance and Rule 37 sanctions for executing a document dump (321 F.R.D. 303), and summary disallowance of its Regular Research Credit base period for relying on unsubstantiated assertions regarding 1980s T&M contracts (2019 WL 250602).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Historical Base Period Audit and Protective ASC Election Protocol

Unlike QHI in Quebe, which claimed the § 41(c)(3)(B) start-up method and then, in litigation, relied solely on a consultant’s hearsay testimony that its predecessor’s 1980s contracts were primarily T&M, Vanguard must conduct a rigorous Pre-Filing Evidentiary Audit of its Legacy Subsidiaries’ 1984–1988 records under Federal Rules of Evidence 803(6) (Business Records Exception) and 803(16) (Ancient Documents Exception). To legally sustain the position under IRC § 41(c)(3)(B) or § 41(c)(3)(A) that 1984–1988 work was excluded as "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), Vanguard’s tax counsel must verify that the company possesses complete audited financial statements and Forms 1120 for 1984–1988 establishing total gross receipts for all three Legacy Subsidiaries, alongside the actual contemporaneous 1984–1988 customer contracts, purchase orders, and billing ledgers demonstrating that engineering work during those years was billed strictly on an hourly T&M basis with no technical performance guarantee, authenticated by sworn declarations under Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(4) from original 1980s officers possessing first-hand personal knowledge under Fed. R. Evid. 602. If Vanguard’s archival review reveals any material gap in the 1984–1988 contract records of even one Legacy Subsidiary—which is the expected reality given the 40-year shelf-life problem exposed in Quebe—Vanguard must abandon the Regular Research Credit and elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under IRC § 41(c)(4) on its original timely filed Form 6765. Under Quebe, sacrificing the incremental spread between the 20 percent RRC and the 14 percent ASC is mandatory risk management whenever 1984–1988 predecessor records cannot satisfy federal admissibility standards.
Step 2: Bifurcation of Hybrid Customer Contracts (Defeating Current-Year Funded Research Challenges)

To prevent the IRS from disqualifying Vanguard’s current-year automation projects under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Vanguard must restructure its customer contracting templates to sever R&D phases from non-R&D phases. Vanguard must replace blended MSAs with two distinct Statements of Work (SOWs). SOW Phase I (Custom Robotic Cell & Machine-Vision Algorithm Development — Unfunded R&D) must be structured strictly as a Firm Fixed-Price (FFP) contract tied to quantifiable technical acceptance criteria (such as achieving sub-micron optical defect detection at 120 parts per minute with a <0.01% false-positive rate), containing an explicit Warranty and Rejection Clause under which the client may reject the deliverable and withhold or recover milestone payments if the system fails acceptance testing, and an IP Retention Clause confirming Vanguard retains non-exclusive commercial rights to reuse all underlying kinematics models, vision algorithms, and hardware architectures across its business without royalty obligations. Conversely, SOW Phase II (On-Site Installation, Operator Training, and Post-Acceptance T&M Support — Excluded Non-R&D) must be executed as a separate T&M service agreement, with all labor and materials billed under Phase II automatically flagged as ineligible in Vanguard’s ERP system and excluded from the Section 41 QRE calculation.
Step 3: Technical Uncertainty Demarcation vs. Routine Customer Adaptation (IRC § 41(d)(4)(B))

In custom automation, the IRS routinely contends that engineering efforts merely adapt an existing business component to a particular customer’s requirement—an activity explicitly excluded from qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B). To overcome this objection, at project kickoff (Gate 0), Vanguard’s Lead Systems Engineer must complete a contemporaneous Technical Uncertainty Charter documenting why existing, off-the-shelf vision algorithms and standard robotic kinematics cannot achieve the required throughput or precision due to fundamental physical constraints, such as specular reflection on titanium medical implants causing optical sensor saturation. Throughout development, Vanguard must integrate its Git version-control repository, Jira engineering tickets, and SolidWorks Product Data Management (PDM) logs to automatically archive each alternative optical filtering and neural-network architecture hypothesized, the computer simulations and physical bench-test runs conducted, empirical failure data from rejected iterations, and final validation test results, thereby establishing a structured process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C).
Step 4: Litigation-Grade Discovery and Audit Indexing (Overcoming Quebe, 321 F.R.D. 303)

To remediate the 45,000-page unindexed document production and avoid the sanction regime of United States v. Quebe, 321 F.R.D. 303, and IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F, Vanguard must immediately withdraw the unorganized upload and substitute a structured Master Substantiation Matrix prepared in accordance with Federal Rule of Evidence 1006 (Summaries to Prove Content).

2. Research Activities Performed (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C))

Git Commit Logs; Jira Experimentation Tickets; SolidWorks FEA/Optical Simulation Reports (Bates VAG-00141 to VAG-04800).
3. Individuals Performing Research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B))
Full name, employee ID, W-2 engineering title, department, and statutory qualification role (direct performance, direct supervision, or direct support).
Bi-Weekly Contemporaneous Engineering Timecards; W-2 Payroll Registers (Bates VAG-04801 to VAG-06200).
4. Information Sought to be Discovered (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)–(B))
Specific capability, method, or design uncertainty resolved through engineering principles (e.g., eliminating false-positive optical scatter below 0.01% at 120 ppm).
Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) Protocols; Rejected Iteration Failure Logs (Bates VAG-06201 to VAG-07950).
5. Exact QRE & Contractual Nexus (IRC § 41(b) & § 41(d)(4)(H))
Allocation of qualified wages, prototype supplies, and 65% contract research expenses tied to specific ERP job-cost sub-accounts and unfunded SOW Phase I terms.
Executed SOW Phase I Fixed-Price Contracts; General Ledger Sub-Account Extracts; Vendor Invoices (Bates VAG-07951 to VAG-09500).

body.text: Finally, all written audit and discovery responses accompanying the Master Substantiation Matrix must be personally reviewed, verified, and signed under penalty of perjury by a designated corporate officer of Vanguard alongside the lead engineering records custodian who compiled the Rule 1006 summaries, ensuring full admissibility and procedural compliance in both IRS examination and federal court litigation.
5. Synthesis of Legal and Technical Conclusions

The trilogy of rulings in United States v. Quebe establishes an unforgiving evidentiary standard for taxpayers claiming federal research credits under IRC Section 41 and energy-efficiency deductions under IRC Section 179D. First, corporate taxpayers growing through mergers and acquisitions cannot ignore the pre-acquisition tax histories of acquired subsidiaries under IRC § 41(f); claiming the Regular Research Credit "start-up" method without admissible 1984–1988 records from every acquired predecessor invites summary disallowance, making the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) the essential structural safeguard whenever 40-year-old records are unavailable. Second, taxpayers cannot claim routine construction or engineering operations as qualified research in current years while simultaneously asserting that identical historical operations were non-qualifying or "funded" without contract-specific documentary proof. Third, third-party tax consultants holding contingent-fee arrangements cannot serve as factual declarants for historical or technical operations of which they lack personal knowledge; courts will strike such testimony as inadmissible hearsay under the Federal Rules of Evidence. Finally, both in administrative refund claims under IRS CCA 20214101F and in federal discovery under Quebe (321 F.R.D. 303), volume is never a substitute for structure: taxpayers must maintain contemporaneous, Bates-indexed records that directly link qualified expenditures, technical personnel, and iterative experimentation to discrete business components.

metaDescription: Quebe v. United States: the start-up base period requires admissible evidence that acquired predecessors lacked disqualifying 1984–1988 research.
